title: Coolmath Games
description: Hundreds of browser games, no download needed
review: Coolmath Games has been the office and classroom time sink since the Flash era and it still holds up: hundreds of games that open instantly with no account and no download. The library skews toward puzzle and skill games, which is exactly what you want on a short break. The catch is the ad load — this site is monetised aggressively, so an ad blocker makes a real difference. If you want modern graphics or online matchmaking, look elsewhere; this is deliberately simple stuff.

title: Krunker
description: Fast browser FPS that loads in seconds
review: A browser first-person shooter that loads fast enough to be worth opening on a whim. Matches are short, movement is quick, and there is a proper ranked scene if you get hooked. Runs surprisingly well on a work laptop, though you will want to turn the graphics down on integrated chips. The one thing to know: the skill ceiling is high and the lobby is full of people who have been playing for years, so expect to be bad at it for a while.

title: Slither.io
description: Snake battle royale, two minutes a round
review: The premise takes five seconds to learn: steer a worm, eat glowing dots, grow, and do not run into anyone. Rounds last anywhere from thirty seconds to ten minutes, which is what makes it such a good break game — you can always stop after this one. The difficulty curve is brutal once you get long, because a bigger snake turns slowly and everyone is hunting you. No account, no tutorial, works on a trackpad.

title: Agar.io
description: Eat smaller blobs, grow, don't get eaten
review: The original cell-eating battle royale and still the cleanest version of the idea. You start as a tiny circle, absorb anything smaller than you, and try to survive long enough to matter. Matches are fast and the whole thing is mouse-only, which makes it unusually discreet. Downsides: the leaderboard is dominated by players who team up, which can feel unfair in solo play, and the site runs a fair number of ads around the game canvas.

title: Wordle
description: One five-letter word a day, worldwide
review: One puzzle per day, six guesses, and then you are locked out until tomorrow — which is precisely why it became a daily ritual for millions of people. Because everybody gets the same word, the conversation afterwards is half the point. The enforced scarcity is the feature: there is no way to binge it, so it can never eat your afternoon. Be aware the New York Times version now sits behind their account wall for stats history, and it needs a working connection to their servers.

title: GeoGuessr
description: Guess where in the world the street view is
review: You get dropped into a random Street View location and have to work out where on Earth you are from the sun, the signage, the road markings and the car's roof rack. Genuinely educational in a way that does not feel like education. The free tier only gives you a handful of rounds per day, which is either a frustration or a built-in limit depending on your priorities. Best played with other people in the room — the arguing is the fun part.

title: Skribbl.io
description: Draw and guess with friends or strangers
review: Online Pictionary with a private-room option, which is what makes it useful: create a room, send the link to colleagues, and you have a genuinely good team activity that needs no installs. Drawing with a mouse is deliberately clumsy, and the guessing is timed, so rounds move briskly. Public lobbies can be chaotic and occasionally rude, so use a private room if you are playing with people you know.

title: Little Alchemy 2
description: Combine elements and discover over 700 things
review: Start with four basic elements and combine them to discover hundreds more — fire plus water makes steam, steam plus earth makes a geyser, and so on up the chain. It is a quietly excellent way to spend twenty minutes because progress is visible and there is always one more combination to try. The full list runs past seven hundred items, so it scales from a coffee break to a long evening. Works offline in the browser once loaded, which is handy on a flaky connection.

description: Slide tiles, merge numbers, chase the next power
review: The archetypal one-more-go game: slide tiles on a four-by-four grid, merge matching numbers, and try to reach 2048 without filling the board. It runs on arrow keys, needs no mouse precision, and looks like nothing at all from three desks away, which makes it the most discreet game on this list. The catch is that it is genuinely hard to stop — ten minutes is easy to lose. There is nothing to install and nothing to sign up for.

title: Chess.com
description: Play chess online, with puzzles and lessons
review: The biggest chess site on the internet: rapid games against anyone in the world, a daily puzzle, and an enormous library of opening lessons. The reason it works as a work-break site is that a five-minute blitz game has a natural end — unlike social media, there is no infinite scroll. Free accounts get a limited number of daily puzzles and no deep game analysis; the paid tier is what unlocks the study tools. Time controls start at one minute, so be careful which button you press.

title: Lichess
description: Free open-source chess, no ads, no paywall
review: Everything chess.com does, run as a non-profit and funded by donations, which means no ads and no premium upsell anywhere on the site. The interface is plainer but faster, and the analysis board is completely free, which is unusual. If you want to play a few games without being advertised at, this is the one to bookmark. The pool of players is a little smaller than the big commercial site, so matchmaking at odd hours or exotic time controls can take longer.

title: Shell Shockers
description: Egg-themed browser FPS, runs in a tab
review: You are an egg with a gun. That is the whole pitch, and it works better than it has any right to: fast rounds, several weapons, and a surprisingly active player base for something that runs in a browser tab with no download. Good for a quick competitive fix. The art style is cartoonish enough that a passing glance reads as a harmless animation rather than a shooter, which is either convenient or a genuine concern depending on your workplace.

title: Squaredle
description: A daily word-search puzzle on a grid
review: Find every word hidden in a grid of letters, with a fresh puzzle each day and a harder weekend edition. It scratches the same itch as a crossword but is easier to pick up and put down, and like the best daily puzzles it is finite — there is a defined end, which protects your afternoon. A hint system exists for when you are one word short and about to give up. Works fine on a phone, so it is a good commute option too.

title: Diep.io
description: Drive a tank, upgrade it, shoot everything
review: The concept is a tank that grows: destroy shapes and other players, spend points on upgrades, and pick a class branch that changes how you play. There are enough build combinations to make it interesting for a lot longer than the simple graphics suggest. Rounds are quick and there is no sign-up. It is more mechanically demanding than the other io games here, so it is less forgiving if you have only got one hand free.

title: Zombs Royale
description: 2D battle royale with five-minute matches
review: A top-down battle royale that condenses the whole hundred-player formula into a match you can finish before your coffee gets cold. Loot, shrink zone, last one standing — all the beats are there, just at ten times the speed. It is genuinely good at the thing it is trying to do. On the downside the player base is smaller than it once was, so some lobbies will be filled with bots, which is either great for your win rate or a bit hollow.

title: Sudoku.com
description: Sudoku with difficulty levels and a clean board
review: A straightforward, well-built sudoku site with six difficulty levels and a clean board that does not try to sell you anything on top. The beginner and easy tiers are genuinely quick, and the expert tier will eat a lunch break on its own. There are number-pad controls and a pencil-mark mode for candidates, which is what you need once puzzles get hard. The strongest point for an office setting is that a sudoku grid is the least suspicious thing anyone can be looking at.

title: Gartic Phone
description: Telephone game played with drawings
review: The telephone game, but each person draws what they were told and then describes what they were shown, producing a slideshow of escalating nonsense by the end. Needs at least three or four people to work, and it is by far the best of the multiplayer drawing games if you can get a group together. Private rooms are free and there is no download. Result images are shareable, which is half the payoff.

title: Monkeytype
description: Minimal typing test, quietly addictive
review: A typing speed test with a stripped-back interface and a serious amount of customisation hidden underneath — you can choose word lists, languages, punctuation, code snippets, even quote sources. It tracks your words per minute and accuracy over time and shows where your weak keys are. Upgrading your typing is a legitimately useful way to spend ten minutes, which makes it one of the few things on this list you could mention to your manager without lying.

title: The Useless Web
description: Throws you at a random pointless website
review: One button, and it takes you to a random website that has no reason to exist — a screaming goat, a page that just plays a single noise, a site that does one inexplicable thing very well. It is the original of this genre and still the best introduction to it. Ideal for the moment when you want to look at something absurd for ninety seconds and then get back to work. Some destinations are loud, so check your volume first.

title: Bored Button
description: Hit the button, land somewhere entertaining
review: Curated rather than random: every press sends you to a small interactive toy, game or oddity that has been vetted for being worth the stop. That makes the hit rate noticeably higher than the pure-random equivalents, and you can go several presses deep without hitting a dud. There is a proper 404-like dead-end from time to time. Good for when you want to be shown something rather than to choose it.

title: Pointer Pointer
description: Photos of people pointing at wherever your cursor is
review: Move your mouse anywhere on the page and it finds a photograph of somebody pointing at that exact spot. That is all it does, and the technical trick behind it is more interesting than the result — a database of photos indexed by where in the frame the pointing hand is. Best described in one sentence to a colleague, who will then inevitably try it themselves. Harmless, silent, and completely safe to open at work.

title: Neal.fun
description: Interactive experiments and beautiful time sinks
review: A collection of self-contained interactive toys, each one built around a single clever idea: scale yourself against the size of the universe, scroll down through the deep sea by depth, try to draw a perfect circle, or see how far you can make it through a password game with increasingly absurd rules. The quality is consistently high and each piece has a defined end, so it does not turn into an infinite scroll. This is the one to open when you want something genuinely well made.

title: Windows 93
description: A fake operating system stuffed with secrets
review: An entire fictional operating system rendered in the browser, complete with a working file explorer, a music player, games, and a long tail of jokes hidden behind almost every icon. Half the fun is clicking things to find out whether they do anything. It is a genuinely impressive piece of web art that happens to look completely innocuous from a distance. Modern browsers handle it fine, but it needs sound enabled to get the full effect, so be careful with speakers.

title: Zoomquilt
description: An illustration you can zoom into forever
review: A collaborative painting that loops seamlessly into itself — the image is always zooming in, and the detail never runs out because the artwork wraps around. The effect is hypnotic and slightly unsettling, which is exactly the point. It runs by itself with no interaction, so it works well as moving background art on a second monitor. If you are prone to motion sickness from visual loops, this one may not be for you.

title: Staggering Beauty
description: Shake the cursor and watch it go berserk
review: A hairy worm follows your cursor, and if you shake it enough the whole thing explodes into flashing colour and a noise that is much louder than you expect. The site is a single joke, but it is a well-timed one, and the warning about the sound is not a formality. Do not open this one with the volume up in an open-plan office. It is also a piece of early web-art history, which is a decent excuse for having it bookmarked.

title: Cat Bounce
description: Bounce a screenful of cats around
review: Click to spawn a cat, watch it fall, bounce, and eventually drift off the bottom of the screen. You can add as many as your machine will tolerate, at which point the whole thing becomes an absurd physics demonstration. There is no score, no goal and no end, which on a bad day is exactly the right amount of pressure. Completely silent by default, so it is safe to leave open.

title: Endless Horse
description: A horse with no bottom in sight
review: An ASCII horse that simply does not end — the legs keep going, no matter how far you scroll. The joke lands immediately and there is nothing else to do here, which somehow makes it better: it is a statement about the internet itself. Takes two seconds to load and costs you thirty seconds of attention. A useful thing to send to someone who has just asked you to look at something pointless.

title: This Is Sand
description: Pour coloured sand and make something
review: Click and hold to pour sand, let gravity settle it, and build up coloured layers into something that looks surprisingly deliberate. There is a full colour picker and the results are genuinely attractive, which makes it a better creative break than it sounds. Works well on a tablet. No account and no saving by default — if you make something you like, screenshot it before you close the tab, because it will be gone.

title: Wait But Why
description: Long illustrated essays about big questions
review: Deep, carefully argued essays with stick-figure illustrations, covering everything from why procrastination works the way it does to what happens when artificial intelligence arrives. The pieces are long by design — an hour is a normal length, which makes them a poor fit for a five-minute break but excellent company over lunch. The writing is unusually clear about its own uncertainty, which is rarer than it should be.

title: Is It Christmas?
description: Answers exactly one question, correctly
review: A single page that answers one yes-or-no question, and gets it right. For 364 days a year the answer is no. There is nothing else here at all, which is precisely the joke, and there is a certain satisfaction in a website that has been quietly maintained for over a decade to do nothing but tell the truth once a year. Loads instantly, works on any device.

title: Wiby
description: A search engine for the old, hand-made web
review: Wiby deliberately indexes the un-commercial corner of the web: personal homepages, hobby sites, text pages, things built in the late nineties by one person on a static HTML file. Searching it feels like the internet did before everything got optimised, and the surprise-me button reliably lands somewhere you would never find otherwise. Nothing about it is slick, and that is the point. Excellent for a genuinely unexpected five minutes.

title: The Nicest Place
description: Strangers waving at the camera, on loop
review: A rotating gallery of short clips of people smiling and waving directly at the camera. No music, no captions, no framing — just ordinary people being friendly. It is the single most effective antidote to a bad afternoon on this entire list, and it takes about forty seconds. Silent by default so it is safe to leave open, though you will probably want the sound off anyway.

title: Window Swap
description: Look out of a stranger's window somewhere else
review: People around the world upload short clips of the view from their window, and you get served one at random — a rainy street in Seoul, a balcony in Lisbon, a garden in Vermont. It is a genuinely lovely use of the internet and a much more restful form of travel than a feed. Video quality varies a lot depending on who uploaded it, and the site depends on people continuing to contribute, so it can go quiet.

title: Line Rider
description: Draw a track and send a sled down it
review: Freehand draw a line, drop a sled at the top, and watch physics take over — which is fun for thirty seconds and then, if the bug bites, genuinely absorbing for entire evenings. The community has produced tracks that are closer to engineering than play, and the editor has enough tools to get you there. The original Flash version is also archived, though the modern build is the one to use. Quiet, no account, saves locally.

title: Weavesilk
description: Symmetrical light painting with your mouse
review: Whatever you drag, it mirrors into a symmetrical glowing form, and the results look considerably more artistic than the effort involved. You can change the symmetry axis and colour palette, and turn on a colour cycle that makes everything move. It is the best of the drawing toys for people who cannot draw, because the symmetry does the hard work. Results are not saved, so screenshot anything you want to keep.

title: Patatap
description: Your keyboard becomes a noise-making instrument
review: Every letter key triggers a shape and a sound, and holding down a rhythm in the right order can sound genuinely musical. There are several sound packs to switch between, so the initial novelty lasts longer than you would expect. It is a better break activity than it looks, mostly because your hands are already on the keyboard. Turn the volume down before you start experimenting.

title: Fake Update
description: Full-screen fake system update screens
review: Full-screen, pixel-accurate fake update screens for Windows, macOS, and a selection of genuinely alarming variants including the classic blue screen. Press F11 for full screen, and from any distance your machine looks like it is doing something important and unavoidable. This is the most effective single decoy on the internet and it has been for years. Obviously, do not leave it up when you actually need your computer.

title: Hacker Typer
description: Mash keys, screens fill with code
review: Press any key and convincing-looking source code streams out at impossible speed, complete with the occasional dramatic access-granted popup. Nobody who knows anything about programming will be fooled for more than a second, but from across a room it reads as intense technical work. There are several themes, including a proper terminal look. The sound effects are off by default, which is the correct decision.

title: Keybr
description: Typing trainer that looks like real training
review: A typing tutor that adapts to your weak letters, generating nonsense words built from the keys you keep getting wrong. It looks and behaves like a professional training tool, which means nobody questions you spending twenty minutes on it — and it genuinely does make you faster. The statistics page tracks your progress by key, which is oddly satisfying to watch improve. Free, no account needed, works offline once loaded.

title: Hemingway Editor
description: Highlights hard-to-read sentences in your writing
review: Paste in a paragraph and it flags the sentences that are too long, the passive voice, the adverbs and the phrases that could be cut. The interface is clean and the feedback is immediate, which makes the whole thing feel like careful editing even when you are mostly watching colours appear. Genuinely useful for writing anything a human will read. The free version does everything in a single pass; the paid tier adds saving and export.

title: ZenPen
description: Distraction-free writing, plain white and black
review: A full-screen text editor with no toolbar, no sidebar and no notifications — just white space and a cursor. That minimalism is also what makes it a perfect background: from a distance it is indistinguishable from any document you might plausibly be working on. Basic formatting exists but is hidden until you ask for it. Text is not saved anywhere, so copy it out before closing the tab.

title: Online Notepad
description: A plain page of text, nothing else
review: A web notepad with no features to speak of, which is exactly the point. White background, black text, no logos shouting for attention, no auto-saving to somewhere you do not control. If you want the least suspicious possible thing to have open on screen while you think, this is it. Content stays in the browser tab only — closing it loses everything, so paste anything worth keeping into a real document first.

title: Virtual Piano
description: Play piano from your keyboard
review: Maps your keyboard to a full piano keyboard, so pressing letters plays notes. There is a large library of sheet music transcribed into letter sequences, including a lot of pop and film themes, so you can learn an actual recognisable tune in a few minutes rather than just making noise. The sample quality is decent for a free browser instrument. Keep the volume low — a piano solo is not subtle in an open-plan office.

title: Grammarly
description: Grammar and tone checking as you write
review: A writing assistant that checks grammar, clarity, tone and wordiness, either as an editor you paste into or as a browser extension. The reason it belongs in this category is that spending fifteen minutes polishing an email looks, from any angle, like taking work seriously — and it is arguably true. The free tier covers correctness well; suggestions about tone and delivery are behind the subscription. Sign-up required for the web editor.

title: TinyPNG
description: Shrink PNG and JPEG files without visible loss
review: Drag in an image, get it back substantially smaller with no visible difference. The compression is smart enough that a screenshot or photograph usually drops by half or more, and you can process up to twenty files at once for free. This is the single most useful utility on this site for anyone who has ever had to email a screenshot. It keeps the transparency in PNGs, which a lot of compressors do not.

title: remove.bg
description: Cut the background out of any photo in one click
review: Upload a photo and the subject is separated from the background automatically, with no manual masking at all. It handles hair and soft edges far better than the crude tools most people have used, and it takes about five seconds. Free downloads are at lower resolution, which is fine for a slide deck and not fine for print. If you want a similar job done by hand with full control, Photopea is the alternative.

title: Squoosh
description: Compress images with a live before-and-after view
review: Drop in an image and drag a slider to see the compressed result update in real time next to the original, which makes it much easier to judge how far you can push a file size before it starts to look bad. Supports modern formats like WebP and AVIF, and runs entirely in your browser so nothing is uploaded anywhere. Built by Google and still one of the better tools of its kind.

title: Photopea
description: Photoshop in a browser tab, opens PSD files
review: An astonishingly complete image editor that runs in a browser and opens Photoshop files with layers intact. If you only need to crop, retouch or export something occasionally, there is no reason to buy an image editor subscription for that. It supports layer masks, adjustment layers, smart objects and a long list of filters. Free with ads on the side of the interface, or a small paid tier to remove them.

title: Excalidraw
description: Hand-drawn style whiteboard for diagrams
review: A whiteboard that makes everything you draw look pleasingly hand-made, which sounds cosmetic until you notice how much more willing people are to comment on a diagram that does not look finished. Excellent for architecture sketches, flowcharts and explaining an idea in a meeting. Supports live collaboration through a share link with no sign-up, and exports to PNG and SVG. The hand-drawn style can be turned off if you want clean lines.

title: WeTransfer
description: Send large files without an account
review: Upload a file, get a link, send the link. No account on either side, up to a couple of gigabytes free per transfer. It is the fastest way to get a big file to somebody who is not on the same chat app as you. Files expire after a few days, which is a feature rather than a bug for one-off sends but means you should not use it for anything archival. Advertising on the download page is heavy on the free tier.

title: iLovePDF
description: Merge, split, compress and convert PDFs
review: A complete set of PDF tools in one place: merge several documents, split one apart, compress a file that is too big to email, or convert to and from Word, Excel and images. The interface is plain and the processing is fast. Free tier limits the number of files per job to keep the paid plan sellable, but for occasional use you will rarely hit it. Uploaded files are deleted from their servers after a couple of hours.

title: CloudConvert
description: Convert between almost any file format
review: The format converter to reach for when the thing you have is in a format the thing you need does not accept — video, audio, document, spreadsheet, ebook or image, in almost any combination. It handles the obscure corners other converters ignore, and will happily extract audio from a video or turn a presentation into images. Free conversions are limited by a daily quota measured in minutes, so large video jobs are the thing you will notice.

title: Regex101
description: Build and debug regular expressions with explanations
review: Paste in a regular expression and some test text and it highlights the matches live, then explains the pattern token by token in plain language on the right. That explanation panel is the reason to use it over anything else — it turns an unreadable string of symbols into something you can actually reason about. Supports the flavours used across most languages. Invaluable if you only write regex occasionally and always forget the syntax.

title: Carbon
description: Turn code into a shareable image
review: Paste in a snippet and it renders it as a nicely framed image with a window chrome, syntax highlighting and configurable colours. This became the standard way to share code on social media, and it is still the most polished of the options. You can set the language, theme, padding and background transparent for use over other designs. There is no account and nothing is uploaded.

title: Ray.so
description: Code screenshots with a cleaner modern look
review: Does the same job as Carbon with a more contemporary aesthetic — soft gradients, neat rounded windows, and sensible defaults that mean you do not need to fiddle with anything before exporting. Supports several languages and both light and dark themes, and the output is sized for social sharing out of the box. If you have ever spent five minutes tweaking a code screenshot, this is the tool that removes that step.

title: Coolors
description: Generate colour palettes by pressing space
review: Press the space bar and a fresh five-colour palette appears; lock the ones you like and keep generating around them. It solves the specific problem of needing colours that work together without knowing anything about colour theory. You can export palettes for design tools, check contrast ratios for accessibility, and pick colours straight out of a photograph. Fast enough to use during a meeting.

title: Unsplash
description: Free high-resolution photos, no attribution needed
review: A large library of professionally shot photographs released under a licence that allows commercial use without attribution or payment. The quality is high enough that a slide deck or landing page looks properly designed with no budget at all. Search works on subject, colour and orientation, which is more useful than it sounds when you need a horizontal image with a lot of empty space for text. Attribution is not required but is appreciated by the photographers.

title: Pexels
description: Free stock photos and video clips
review: Similar licence to Unsplash with the same no-attribution, commercial-use terms, but with a much stronger video section — free stock footage is genuinely hard to find and this is one of the few places that does it well. The photo library is smaller but has plenty of practical business and lifestyle imagery. Useful when you need a ten-second clip as background for something and have no budget.

title: Temp Mail
description: Disposable email address, no sign-up
review: Gives you a working email address instantly that self-destructs after a while, which is what you want for the many sites that demand an address before letting you read anything. The inbox updates live and attachments work. Be sensible about it: never use a disposable address for anything you might need to recover later, since anyone who guesses the address can read the inbox. Great for one-off downloads, terrible for account recovery.

title: tldraw
description: Instant infinite whiteboard, no sign-up
review: Opens straight into an infinite canvas you can draw on immediately, with no login wall and no onboarding. It is more freeform than Excalidraw and better suited to thinking out loud than to producing a polished diagram. There is a good selection of shapes, arrows and sticky notes, and you can share a live session with a link. Perfect for the case where you need to explain something in two minutes and do not want to open a heavy design tool.

title: Reddit
description: The internet's biggest forum, every topic has a home
review: A forum for essentially every subject that has ever interested a human being, from professional specialisms to deeply obscure hobbies. The reason it is dangerous during work hours is not the front page — it is that any specific subreddit is a bottomless archive of genuinely interesting material. Use it deliberately: go to the subreddit you actually want, rather than letting the home feed choose for you. The mobile web version pushes the app aggressively.

title: Hacker News
description: Minimal tech news board, exceptional comments
review: A plain list of links, no images, no tracking, no design to speak of — and the single best comment section on the internet for anything technical. The front page moves slowly enough to check twice a day, and the discussion often contains more insight than the linked article. It is also perfectly camouflaged in an office: to anyone walking past it looks like a plain text file. Submissions skew toward engineering and startups.

title: Product Hunt
description: Daily leaderboard of new products
review: Every day a fresh leaderboard of newly launched software and hardware, each with a short pitch and a comments thread from the makers. It is the fastest way to see what is being built right now, and the useful signal is usually in the comments rather than the ranking. Practically valuable if you work anywhere near product, and quietly entertaining even if you do not. Voting requires an account.

title: Techmeme
description: Tech news curated and clustered by an editor
review: An editor reads the entire tech press and clusters the day's stories into headline threads with links to every outlet covering them, so you can see both the story and the spread of coverage in one glance. It is the most efficient way to find out what actually happened in the industry today. Density is high and there is no design flair whatsoever, which is exactly what you want from an aggregator.

title: Lobsters
description: Small, quiet, technical link community
review: A link-sharing community that stays deliberately small and somewhat invitation-linked, which keeps the quality of both submissions and comments unusually high. The focus is squarely on computing — languages, systems, tooling — with less of the startup news that dominates other boards. Posts move slowly, so checking it twice a day is enough, and the low traffic means you can actually read everything. A good complement to Hacker News rather than a replacement for it.

title: Digg
description: Curated tech and internet culture stories
review: The rebooted Digg is a small editorial operation rather than a voting site, and it works better for it: a handful of genuinely interesting stories each day about technology, the internet and the odd things happening on it. There is none of the endless-feed pressure of bigger aggregators, so ten minutes on it has a natural end. Good for the moment when you want to know what people are talking about without opening a social network.

title: Google Trends
description: What the world is searching for right now
review: Shows what search terms are spiking, broken down by country and time range, with related queries and regional interest. It is genuinely useful for understanding why something is suddenly everywhere, and quietly good fun for comparing the relative popularity of two things across countries. The data is normalised rather than absolute, so treat the numbers as relative interest rather than search volume. No account needed to browse.

title: Slashdot
description: The original tech news site, running since 1997
review: One of the oldest continuously running sites on the web, still posting a handful of editor-selected technology stories a day with a comment thread underneath. The community is smaller and older than it once was, but that is part of the appeal — the discussion is knowledgeable and slow-moving. Its plain, text-heavy layout is also ideal for looking unremarkable on a work screen.

title: The Verge
description: Technology news with strong visual design
review: A mainstream technology publication with a distinctive visual style, strong opinion writing and good coverage of the consumer end of tech — phones, gadgets, streaming, and the culture around them. The layout is image-heavy, which makes it more obviously leisure reading than a text-based news site, so it is one for lunch rather than a sneaky tab. Their long-form features are where the quality really shows.

title: Ars Technica
description: Deep technology reporting and analysis
review: Serious technology journalism with more technical depth than the general press — long pieces on security research, processor architecture, spaceflight and policy, written by people who clearly understand the subject. The comment section is well moderated and often adds real expertise. Articles are long, so this is a lunch-break site rather than a five-minute one, and the depth means it doubles as legitimate professional reading.

title: YouTube
description: Everything from long documentaries to ten-second clips
review: The obvious answer to almost any video need: full-length documentaries, conference talks, ambient background footage, and an effectively infinite supply of short distracting clips. The recommendation feed is engineered to be hard to leave, so the practical advice is to search for the specific thing you want rather than opening the homepage. Background play works in a browser tab, which makes it usable as an audio source while you do something else.

title: Twitch
description: Live streaming, good as background company
review: Live streams of people playing games, making music, coding, painting or just talking. The reason it belongs on a list like this is the ambient use case: a stream running in a corner of the screen provides company and a low-level sense of activity without demanding attention. Plenty of channels are quiet and chat-free, which is the mode you want. Live video is bandwidth-hungry, so it is the thing to close first if your connection is struggling.

title: Spotify Web Player
description: The full Spotify library in a browser tab
review: The complete Spotify catalogue without installing the desktop application — useful on a locked-down work machine where you cannot install software. Playlists, search and the various mood and genre stations all work. The free tier runs advertising and limits how many tracks you can skip, and it occasionally will not play a specific track on demand. Works well alongside a focus playlist for a long stretch of work.

title: SoundCloud
description: Where independent musicians upload first
review: The place unsigned and independent artists post music, which means an enormous amount of material that exists nowhere else — remixes, live sets, DJ mixes, demos that never got a proper release. Following a few artists gives you a feed that is genuinely different from any streaming service's algorithm. The downside is quality control: there is a lot of everything, including rough recordings and abandoned uploads.

title: Bandcamp
description: Independent music you can stream in full
review: Artists upload albums and you can stream them in full before deciding, which is increasingly rare — most platforms give you thirty seconds and a nag. The catalogue leans toward independent, experimental and niche music, and buying anything sends a genuinely large share of the money to the artist. Many albums are free or pay-what-you-want. The discovery tools are weak, so it works best when you already know what you are looking for.

title: Internet Archive
description: Old films, music, software and web pages
review: A non-profit library holding an enormous and slightly chaotic collection: public domain films, live concert recordings, old software, radio broadcasts, and snapshots of websites going back to the nineties. The Wayback Machine alone justifies a bookmark, letting you see what any site looked like years ago. Search is imprecise and quality varies wildly, but there is genuinely nothing else like it. Everything is free to browse.

title: Tubi
description: Free films and TV, funded by advertising
review: A free, ad-supported streaming service with a much deeper catalogue than its low profile suggests — a lot of older films, cult titles and complete series runs that the paid platforms have dropped. No account is needed to start watching. The trade-off is advertising, and there is a fair amount of it. Worth checking before renting anything, because the odds are decent that it is already sitting here for free.

title: Pluto TV
description: Free live TV channels that just keep playing
review: Works like broadcast television: a list of themed channels that are always running, so you drop into whatever is on rather than choosing something. That is the appeal — no browsing, no decision fatigue, and you cannot binge because the schedule decides. Mostly older series and films, with a surprising number of niche channels devoted to single subjects. Free and ad-supported, no account required.

title: Radio Garden
description: Spin a globe and tune into any country's radio
review: A 3D globe covered in thousands of green dots, each one a live radio station — click anywhere and you are listening to local radio in Reykjavik, Lagos or rural Brazil. It is the most elegant idea on this list and it turns listening to the radio into an act of exploration. Stations are contributed via a community project, so some streams are dead or buffer badly, but the hit rate is high enough to keep going. No account needed.

title: NTS Radio
description: London radio station with excellent curation
review: An independent online radio station with two always-on channels and an enormous archive of past shows, all mixed by people with genuinely good taste across jazz, electronic, ambient, hip-hop and things that do not have a genre name. The shows are long and uninterrupted, which makes it ideal to leave running while you work. The archive is searchable by mood and genre, so you can find a two-hour mix for exactly the afternoon you are having.

title: Letterboxd
description: Track films you've watched, read good short reviews
review: Part diary, part social network: log what you watch, rate it, and read short reviews from people who take films seriously without taking themselves too seriously. The lists feature is the quiet star — searching for a specific theme reliably turns up a curated list somebody has spent real time on. Useful for deciding what to watch tonight, and dangerous as a general browsing activity, because the reviews are genuinely entertaining.

title: Rainy Mood
description: Looping rain, the classic focus sound
review: The original single-purpose rain loop, and still the most reliable — one page, one sound, no controls to fiddle with. Rain is unusually good at masking office noise because it covers the frequency range of conversation without competing for attention. Keep it at low volume and it disappears into the background within a minute. There is a paid app, but the website has done the job for over a decade without one.

title: A Soft Murmur
description: Mix rain, thunder, wind and café noise
review: Rather than one fixed sound, this gives you a set of sliders — rain, thunder, waves, wind, fire, birds, café chatter, white noise — that you blend yourself. The mixing is the point: matching the sound to your mood takes a few seconds and makes it much less likely you will switch it off. There is a timer for sessions, and settings you can share as a link. Works well on a phone too.

title: Noisli
description: Background noise generator with a built-in timer
review: Combines a sound mixer with a text editor and a pomodoro timer, so the whole focus session lives in one tab: choose your soundscape, set twenty-five minutes, write. The interface is calm and does not try to gamify anything. Palettes are saved between visits, which removes the friction of rebuilding your mix every day. The free tier is generous; the paid tier adds offline use and playback on more devices.

title: MyNoise
description: Professional-grade noise generators you can tune
review: The most sophisticated sound generator here by some distance: dozens of carefully recorded soundscapes, each with a graphic equaliser you can adjust across ten frequency bands, so you can add or remove exactly the frequencies that distract you. Built by an audio engineer and it shows. Genuinely useful for anyone sensitive to specific noises, like nearby speech or keyboard clatter. Everything is free, funded by donations.

title: Lofi Cafe
description: Lo-fi radio with a lovely interface
review: A handful of always-on lo-fi channels, each with a slightly different mood, wrapped in an interface that is a pleasure to look at — animated backgrounds and a clean player that sits quietly in the corner. Lo-fi works as work music because it has enough texture to mask noise but not enough melodic content to pull your attention. Free, no account, runs happily in a background tab for hours.

title: Chillhop
description: Official Chillhop radio, live around the clock
review: The label behind a lot of the lo-fi you have heard on study playlists runs its own 24-hour stream, plus a catalogue of releases you can browse. The music is jazz-influenced instrumental hip-hop, consistently well produced, and the live stream means you never have to choose a track. A solid default for a long stretch of focused work. There is also a seasonal playlist that changes what is on air.

title: Music for Programming
description: Mixes built specifically for deep work
review: A long-running series of hour-long mixes, each accompanied by a page of notes about the music and about programming. The selections avoid lyrics and obvious hooks, which is exactly the property that makes them hold up over a two-hour stretch. There is no player chrome to distract you and no algorithm making decisions — you pick an episode and it plays. A cult favourite for a reason.

title: Poolsuite FM
description: Retro summer radio with a 1980s holiday vibe
review: An internet radio station styled as a 1980s resort advertisement — sun-drenched graphics, old-school typography, and a soundtrack of relaxed funk, disco and synth. The whole page is a small piece of design work, which makes it a pleasure to leave open. The music is exactly the holiday-adjacent mood it promises. Skip it if what you actually need is silence rather than atmosphere.

title: Explore.org
description: Live cameras on animals around the world
review: A network of live cameras pointed at wildlife — bears fishing at a waterfall, eagles in a nest, kittens in a shelter, a coral reef — running continuously with no commentary. It is the most effective thing here for bringing your heart rate down, and it is genuinely well produced by a non-profit foundation. Cameras occasionally go offline or show a static view for hours, particularly overnight, so try a couple.

title: Wikipedia
description: The encyclopedia that eats entire afternoons
review: You know what it is; the reason it belongs on this list is the specific hazard of the link chains. Open one article and follow the tangents and you will surface forty minutes later with a working knowledge of something completely unrelated to your job. The citation sections are the genuinely valuable part — they are a curated reading list on whatever you just looked up. Available in hundreds of languages, ad-free and donation-funded.

title: Khan Academy
description: Free structured courses from arithmetic to calculus
review: A complete, free curriculum covering maths, science, economics, history and more, with video explanations and exercises that adapt to what you keep getting wrong. The maths track in particular is far better than most paid alternatives, and it goes genuinely deep. Progress tracking makes it a real study tool rather than a video library. Entirely free, run as a non-profit, no advertising.

title: Coursera
description: University courses you can sit in on for free
review: Courses from universities and companies, most of which can be audited for free — the paid part buys you a certificate and graded assignments, not the lectures. The range is enormous, from introductory programming to quite specialist graduate material, and the best courses have genuinely good production values. Commitment is the thing to watch: many courses run for weeks, so it is worth checking the syllabus before starting one at the beginning of a busy period.

title: edX
description: Academic courses from MIT, Harvard and others
review: A non-profit platform carrying courses from major universities, with a more academic tone than its commercial equivalents — you will find rigorous treatments of subjects that other platforms skip. Many courses can be audited free, with paid verification for certificates. The discussion forums on the better courses are worth reading on their own. Expect real workload if you actually do the assignments.

title: Brilliant
description: Learn maths and science by solving problems
review: Teaches concepts through short interactive problems instead of lectures, which turns out to be a much better fit for a ten-minute break — you make progress in the time you have rather than watching half a video. Covers maths, logic, physics, computer science and data. The free tier gives you a limited number of problems a day, so the subscription is what unlocks the full paths. Genuinely well designed.

title: MIT OpenCourseWare
description: MIT course materials, free and permanent
review: MIT publishes the actual materials from thousands of its courses — lecture notes, problem sets, exams with solutions, and recordings of lectures where they exist. It is not a guided course; you get the raw material and decide what to do with it. For anyone who wants to see what a serious undergraduate treatment of a subject looks like, this is unmatched and completely free with no registration.

title: Duolingo
description: Learn a language in ten-minute daily sessions
review: The gamification is what makes it work: streaks, leagues and daily goals turn language practice into something you actually return to, which matters more than pedagogy for the first few months. The courses vary in quality — the major European languages are much stronger than the less common ones. Ten minutes a day is the designed unit, and it is a genuinely good use of a coffee break. The free tier is fully usable; the subscription removes ads and adds practice tools.

title: Wolfram Alpha
description: A computation engine, not a search engine
review: Ask it a question with a definite answer and it computes rather than searches: solve an equation, differentiate a function, plot data, convert units, check a date, look up a physical constant. It shows the steps for many mathematical problems, which makes it genuinely useful for checking your own working rather than just getting an answer. Typing in plain English mostly works, though precise notation gives much better results.

title: Our World in Data
description: Global problems explained through charts
review: Research and data on the big global questions — energy, health, population, poverty, food, climate — organised as readable articles built around well-made charts, with the underlying data downloadable. The tone is unusually careful: it reports what the evidence supports and explicitly flags where it does not. A good antidote to the confident half-truths that circulate on the same subjects. Free, non-profit, no paywall.

title: Atlas Obscura
description: A map of the world's strangest places
review: A collaboratively built atlas of unusual places and phenomena: a lake that turns animals to stone, a library of smells, the world's loneliest tree, tunnels you can visit under a city. Every entry is short enough to read in a minute, which makes it dangerously easy to read twenty in a row. The map view is excellent for finding oddities near somewhere you are actually travelling to. Free to browse, with optional membership.
